vignette:
Arisara Tran-or Sara, as she insists her patients call her-built her world on precision. For twenty-five years, her dental practice has been a sanctuary of control and order. The precise angle of a drill, the delicate art of crafting a crown, the satisfying click of a perfectly set inlay-these were the rhythms of her life. Her hands, steady and sure, were her gift. She loved the quiet confidence she could restore in people with her work, transforming pained grimaces into bright, easy smiles. Her life with her husband, Mark, was similarly ordered: comfortable, predictable, and safe.

That sense of safety began to unravel two years ago, starting with a new patient. He was charming at first, then overly complimentary. His praise shifted from her dental work to her hands, her eyes, her smile. Sara, practiced in maintaining a warm but professional barrier, would politely redirect the conversation. But the boundary she held so firmly meant nothing to him. He began leaving notes on her car windshield. Then small, unwanted gifts started arriving at the office-a single rose, a box of chocolates. Her front desk staff were unnerved. Sara felt a cold knot of dread tightening in her stomach.

The fear escalated when he started appearing outside the office, just watching. He was at the grocery store. He was parked down the street from her home. The world, once a predictable map between her practice and her house, became a landscape of potential threats. Every car that slowed down, every man who held her gaze for a second too long, could be him. The police were called, reports were filed, and eventually, a restraining order was issued. He disappeared, but the feeling of being watched did not.

Now, at 51, Sara's world has shrunk to the size of a keyhole. The precision she once commanded has turned against her. Her hands, once so steady, now carry a fine tremor she has to consciously quell before picking up an instrument. Leaning over a male patient, the scent of an unfamiliar cologne can make her breath catch in her throat. For a disorienting second, the man in her chair is replaced by the stalker's face, his eyes holding that same intense, proprietary stare. She has to dig her nails into her own palm to stay grounded in the sterile reality of the operatory, focusing on the minute geography of a tooth until the wave of panic subsides.

She no longer enjoys the small talk that once built rapport with her patients. It feels dangerous, an invitation she can't afford to extend. She finds herself irritable with her assistants over minor things, a misplaced tool or a scheduling error, a frustration that is really a mask for the constant, simmering anxiety. The chime of the front door bell, once an innocuous sound, now sends a jolt of adrenaline through her. Her eyes flick to the security camera monitor a dozen times an hour.

At home, Mark tries to be patient, but he doesn't understand why she still insists on checking the locks three times before bed, or why she flinches when he comes up behind her to wrap his arms around her waist. She feels a profound sense of detachment from him, from the life they built. The joy has been hollowed out, replaced by a dull, persistent vigilance. She hasn't been to their favorite restaurant in over a year because it's on the route the man used to take to her office. She drives a different way to work every single day, the complicated, inefficient routes a small tax she pays to a fear that never sleeps. Her world is orderly once more, but it is the rigid, brittle order of a cage. Every evening, she stands at her living room window, peering through the blinds into the encroaching darkness, a sentry on duty in a war only she is still fighting.
